segments.t: The three most expensive decisions you will make
as a real estate investor are when to sell,
when to refinance, and when to 1031 exchange.
And notice, none of these are when to buy.
Everybody teaches buying,
and there are thousands of hours of free content
on how to find a deal, how to analyze a deal,
even on our site, how to do that.
Also, nobody teaches you what to do with the thing
after you own it, which is a problem,
because that's where most of the money actually is.
It's in the operations,
and it's in the dispose of the property.
If you get these three things right,
you can keep six figures.
If you get these things wrong,
you can hand a lot of it over in closing costs
and to Uncle Sam in taxes very quickly
when you talk about what happens
if you don't choose the right one.
So a quick background for you, right?
I bought a triplex in 2016 in Louisville.
It was a house hack, and since then,
I was able to build up to 30 units in small multifamily.
I built out a short-term rental portfolio,
and I've also built self-storage from the ground up.
I've landed on flips, and my team has helped close
over 180 deals throughout the Metro of Atlanta.
And so what we actually gotta do through here
is give you the details on what we would advise
and what we actually use when it comes to deciding
whether you're gonna sell, refinance,
or 1031 exchange of property into another one.
And so the first rule, when is it the time to sell?
And the time to sell is when you don't have to, right?
There's a famous Warren Buffett quote that says,
to be fearful when others are greedy,
and be greedy when others are fearful.
And so when you look at different time slots,
I'd say that 2020, like late 2020,
all the way through beginning of 2022,
was a time period where it was a seller's market, right?
That's where buyers were jumping over themselves
because the interest rates were so low
to go and buy a property, and that's the time to sell,
right?
And then there's other markets,
like what we're in right now,
where days of market are ticking up.
There's much more inventory,
the interest rate has gone up.
There's a lot less buyers out there,
and this is an opportune time to buy, but not to sell.
If you're listing your property right now,
it should only be if you have to sell it,
and not because, hey, I think I can take some equity out
and things of that nature,
because you're going to have to make concessions
and give up a bit to make that happen
in the market we're in right now.
And so what I look for first and foremost
when it comes to selling is what kind of market are we in?
Are we in a neutral market,
a buyer market, or a seller market?
And for your neutral market, you can go either way, right?
As long as you price it right,
and you list it in the right part of the year,
you should be okay.
If you're in a seller's market,
you should absolutely list that thing.
If there's any properties you're trying to get rid of,
that is the time.
And if you're in a buyer's market,
you should only list if you absolutely have to.
And then there's a couple rules of thumb I have
when buying properties, and then also when disbowing.
When you buy a property, unless you bought it as a flip,
unless you bought it at a discount
where you wanted to do a burr and it needed a lot of work,
or you wanted to do a fix and flip on it,
it wasn't meant to be turned around
and sold two years later, right?
That property, if you wanna build equity
and have enough to where you're gonna pull a profit out,
you need to hold it for a minimum of three to five years,
and ideally five years minimum.
When I buy properties,
I'm looking to hold it for five years to forever, right?
But minimum five years to give time
for that equity to grow,
for that property to get settled and stabilized,
and for it to become even better
than it was when I first bought it.
Because if you get into a property
and then a year or two down the road,
you're like, ah, I think I wanna sell,
and you execute that piece,
what people don't realize is that it costs
a heck of a lot of money to sell a property as well.
From a seller perspective,
it's anywhere from eight to 10% of that purchase price
is what you're going to pay in closing fees,
realtor fees, taxes,
and all those things when you sell a property.
And so if you were to buy a property for,
call it 400K, right?
And then you were to sell that property
two years later or a year later,
let's say for 430K,
you actually lost a little bit of money
when you think about it, right?
If you're at that 10%, you bought it for 400K,
you sold it for 430, you just lost about 43.
So you actually came out net 393, right?
So net, you lost 7K when you factor in
some of the closing costs and things of that nature.
And so it behooves you to hold onto a property
minimum five years.
Because when you look at the historical averages, right?
Even the low historical averages,
if a property is going up by 3% in value
on average every year, right?
Then after you get through year five,
you've gone up at least 15%.
And so at least you're not gonna be out
on your deposit or any of those funds.
You're gonna be actually coming into the green
with some of the funds that you've made.
And if it's been an investment
where you've had somebody else paying that thing off,
you're gonna come way in the green, which is awesome.
And so the rule of thumb here
is if you're gonna calculate roughly,
hey, how much am I going to make on a property
if I sell it?
I use 10% because easy math,
but it's usually a little bit between 8% and 10%
for those costs.
You just wanna take the purchase price
you believe you can sell it for,
subtract 10% and then subtract the remaining mortgage
that you have and that would be your takeaway.
Your takeaway is gonna be a little bit higher than that,
but that's a conservative takeaway for what you would have.
And when you're in a buyer's market,
you may wanna even estimate a little higher
because you're probably gonna give up some concessions
to get your house sold over the others
because there's plenty of stock out there
and other sellers may be a little more desperate than you are
and willing to give concessions
that will pull more buyers in.
And so that's the main thing.
You wanna know what type of market you're in
and then you also want to have that hold time
of minimum five years if possible,
three years, three to five years if possible,
the longer the better.
Now, when do we finance?
We're shifting over.
First, you wanna contact your investor friendly realtor,
have them help you run maybe a CMA
to see, okay, where's the market trending?
What's sold recently?
And see if you have some value in that property.
It's not the end all be all, right?
The end all be all is gonna be the appraiser coming out
to appraise that property,
but at least directionally you can know, okay,
where are we trending based on the market
recently sold around me?
And that's gonna give you a better ballpark
than the Zillow's estimate number, right?
And so after you get that CMA and you see that, okay,
maybe there's some equity in here for refinance.
My whole thing is putting it down on paper
and looking at the payback calculation of the refinance.
When you look at refinance on a property,
the thing that people forget about is
you've gotta pay closing costs again.
You're getting a whole nother mortgage on the property
and that mortgage is essentially gonna pay off
your previous mortgage and replace it.
Now, the reason that you wanna do a refinance
is because it could lower your interest rate,
but there's a calculation that needs to be made for that.
And so if you, when you go to refinance or closing a loan,
it's usually anywhere between two and 5%,
the cost of the property.
I usually just say 3% on average, right?
And that's roughly what it comes out to.
And so if you bought a property for $100,000, right?
And you go to refinance it,
it's gonna cost you roughly $3,000 to refinance it.
And the math that I use to make it worth it
in my own portfolio is the 18 month rule.
For me, if I'm gonna go refinance that $100,000 house
and it's gonna cost me three grand,
I wanna have enough savings from that
that I can recoup that money back in three months or less.
And so let's say you do that refinance
and it's gonna save you $100 per month off of your bill,
but you paid three grand to do it.
It's gonna take you 30 months or two and a half years
before you've recouped the funds
that you put into that refinance.
You probably could have used those funds
for something else, right?
And so if it's two years or more,
I definitely don't want to do it.
If it's in that 18 month mark,
that's when I consider a refinance,
especially if it's a property
I wanna hang on to for a long time.
If it's 36, 48, five years from now,
who knows whether I'm still gonna wanna even hang on
to the property in five years.
If it's gonna take that long
to get the refinance money back,
I typically would not do it
and I'd advise our clients not to do it.
And then when you look at the benefits of refinance,
I can tell you that I just did one
on a quadplex that I have in Gwinnett County
that I've talked about a lot.
When I first bought that property,
because I was in full-time real estate
and I was doing it with like a 1099 loan,
I wanna say my interest rate was like 9%.
It was something crazy,
highest interest rate I've ever had.
When I refinanced it into a DSCR loan this past December,
I was able to take it from 9%
to like 7.3 or something like that.
And long story short,
that dropped my payment by close to $1,000, right?
And so that was well worth it.
I think the refinance itself costs,
I don't know, like 10 grand, something like that.
And to save $1,000 per month,
meaning I can have that whole thing paid off
in 10 months is a major win.
Not to mention,
I actually didn't come out of pocket to pay anything, right?
The money was able to be taken
from the equity in the property
and added to the loan
to pay the loan officer for that refinance.
And so I essentially just lowered my payment,
re-upped the loan.
Yes, it's a little bit longer and things of that nature,
but it's a four-plex where all the tenants
are the ones paying it.
And so that made a lot of sense to me.
Whereas I've had other properties
where I've looked at a refinance and like,
yes, you can drop your interest rate
from like an eight to a seven,
but that's not gonna save you enough
to make the numbers work in my book.
And so the math you wanna run is,
okay, what is a refinance cost?
You wanna go talk to your investor-friendly lender.
How much does a refi cost?
What are the interest rates that I can get?
And then you run the calculation to see,
okay, how many months is it gonna take me
to pay off that refinance?
And is this worth it?
And then the final piece is
when it makes sense to 1031 exchange, okay?
And so let's talk about who a 1031 is for.
And before you even do that, got a disclaimer.
I am not a CPA.
I'm not licensed in that room.
This is just my personal knowledge from going through this.
So please reach out to a CPA if you want the full facts
and that's gonna be the final word.
Definitely talk through CPA.
But 1031 is for an investment property, right?
And this is an opportunity for you to save money
on taxes by selling that property,
not having any of that money touch your account,
and then putting that money into another property
or properties and delaying the payment of those taxes.
And so if you've held a property for a long time, right?
And I'm thinking like a decade plus.
The people before I bought the Quadplex that I purchased,
they had purchased it for 180K back in 2013, right?
And so now consider I'm paying 800K for it.
That's a lot of equity.
I wanna say they 1031ed it into something as well
because they didn't wanna pay six figures in taxes
on the money that they just made
because that's what it'll be.
It'd be like 30, 40% of that you gotta pay toward taxes
depending on what income bracket you're in.
And so that would have been a lot of money.
So they saved that and put it into more property
that's gonna cash flow even more for them, right?
And the game plan has to be,
you have to want to continue investing as well.
You have to see this as a long-term benefit,
real estate investing,
and it's something that you wanna continue doing
if you're gonna do a 1031 exchange
because you're essentially delaying the tax burden
and putting it on another property
that's of equal or greater value
with the intent to continue doing this for a long time
and hopefully pass it down.
And so I actually have a real example
of a client I'm working with right now.
They're based on New York, right?
And this investor bought a property back in like 2010.
They bought a, I think it's like a duplex,
a duplex that has like a commercial rating
and they have a mixed use duplex that has two units
and then underneath it has a commercial space.
I forget what business he said is under there right now,
but he's had it since like the 2010s.
He bought it for 500K in New York.
And right now the value is between 1.2 and 1.5 million.
He has it listed for 1.5
and he's planning to 1031 exchange the funds,
the proceeds from that into property down in Atlanta.
It's probably gonna be two or three properties,
some big multi-families, things of that nature.
But for him, when you look at it,
if he sells this property for where he wants,
he's gonna have a $1 million gain, right?
If you were to pay taxes on this
and say it's like the 40% tax bracket,
you're paying $400,000 to Uncle Sam, right?
This instance makes perfect sense
to seek out a 1031 exchange,
especially if you don't need all these funds right now
and if you're looking to continue investing
in real estate and having flow be the thing that gets you,
not just the actual lump sum of cash.
And so when we looked at this,
what he actually needs to live right now,
cause he's gonna use this to ease into retirement.
He's very close to retirement age,
is he needs about 50, 60K, right?
That's what he needs to get through like the next year
while he stabilizes these properties
and then has these properties start to be his retirement plan
that we're looking at for him.
And so what he's gonna do with this
is he's not gonna take the whole million in a gain.
He's gonna take about 900K of that,
1031 exchange it into property
to where he doesn't have to pay tax on it
and then he's going to use the other 100K
and actually take that into his bank account
and pay taxes.
And the taxes are gonna be roughly call it 40 grand,
right, if we're using the same numbers.
And so you go from a $400,000 tax burden
down to like a 40 grand tax burden,
that is not much.
It's not that at all.
And when you look at that,
this is why you would wanna do a 1031 exchange
is so you can continue to roll that tax burden
down the road and not pay it right now.
And so there's other times where it doesn't make sense.
I can tell you that on a couple of the properties
like that 12 flex that I bought in Kentucky,
when I went to go sell that, right,
I think I had at the CPA and I was like,
hey, shot 1031 exchange,

I was still trying to figure it out back then.

hey, I don't know if that makes sense.
